Your description (multiple, nonhealing ulcers on the arms in a desert setting in North Africa) suggests Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis, often due to *Leishmania major* in that region. Management involves confirming the diagnosis.

What to do now:
- Get diagnostic confirmation: ideally PCR with species ID from a lesion sample. Acceptable tests include a slit-skin smear or scraping, punch biopsy, or aspirate.

- Basic wound care: gentle saline cleansing, nonadherent dressings, avoid topical steroids, treat secondary bacterial infection only if present.

Avoid systemic steroids or immunosuppressants until diagnosis is clear.

When to treat versus observe:
- Many *L. major* lesions heal spontaneously over 2–6 months but leave scars.
- Consider treatment for multiple lesions, large lesions, those over sensitive areas, or based on patient preference to reduce scarring.

First-line options for Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis:

Local therapy (preferred for small, uncomplicated lesions):
- Intralesional antimonial injections: Inject into the lesion and beyond the indurated border. Repeat weekly for several sessions.
- Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen: Freeze-thaw cycles every 2–3 weeks.
- Thermotherapy where available.

Systemic therapy (for challenging cases):
- Consult a specialist for appropriate systemic options.

Supportive care and follow-up:
- Clean, cover, and protect from trauma. Expect slow healing; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
- Old World species rarely cause mucosal disease.

Special situations:
- Pregnancy: Consult a specialist for safe options.

Get expert help:
- Seek care with an infectious diseases or dermatology/tropical medicine specialist experienced in leishmaniasis.

Feel free to share more details so I can help tailor the most appropriate guidance.

Your description (multiple, nonhealing ulcers on the arms in a desert setting in North Africa) strongly suggests Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis, most often due to Leishmania major in that region. Management depends on confirming the diagnosis and, if possible, identifying the species, because that guides therapy.

What to do now
- Get diagnostic confirmation: ideally PCR with species ID from a lesion sample. Acceptable first tests include a slit-skin smear or scraping from the active raised border (Giemsa stain for amastigotes), punch biopsy for histology and PCR, or aspirate for culture/PCR.
- Basic wound care: gentle saline cleansing, nonadherent dressings, avoid topical steroids, treat secondary bacterial infection only if present.
- Avoid empiric systemic steroids or immunosuppressants until diagnosis is clear.

When to treat versus observe
- Many L. major lesions heal spontaneously over 2–6 months but leave scars.
- Treat if any of the following: multiple lesions (commonly >3–5), large lesions (>4–5 cm), lesions over joints or cosmetically sensitive areas (face/hands), lymphangitic spread, chronic nonhealing (>3 months), immunosuppression, or patient preference to shorten disease and scarring.

First-line options for Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis
Local therapy (preferred for small, few, uncomplicated lesions)
- Intralesional antimonial injections (meglumine antimoniate or sodium stibogluconate):
  - Inject into the lesion and 1–2 mm beyond the indurated border until blanching.
  - Repeat weekly for about 3–6 sessions. Often combined with cryotherapy.
  - Common effects: pain, local inflammation; systemic toxicity is minimal with intralesional use.
- Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen:
  - 1–2 freeze–thaw cycles per session, every 2–3 weeks for 2–4 sessions.
  - Best for lesions <3 cm and not over thin skin with poor circulation.
- Thermotherapy (localized heat ~50°C applied once) where devices are available.
- Topical paromomycin (if accessible): 15% paromomycin combinations applied daily for 20–30 days can work for L. major; skin irritation is common. Availability varies by country.

Systemic therapy (consider for multiple/large lesions, difficult sites, failed local therapy, or immunosuppression)
- Meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) or sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam):
  - 20 mg/kg/day of pentavalent antimony (SbV) IM/IV for 20 days.
  - Monitor: ECG (QT prolongation), pancreatic enzymes, LFTs, CBC, creatinine. Adverse effects: myalgias, arthralgias, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity.
- Miltefosine (where available):
  - 2.5 mg/kg/day orally (max 150 mg/day) for 28 days; adults ≥45 kg often 50 mg three times daily with food.
  - Effective for many L. major infections; less predictable for L. tropica.
  - Contraindicated in pregnancy; strict contraception required (women during treatment and for 5 months after; men during treatment and for 3 months after). Adverse effects: GI upset, transaminitis, creatinine rise, rare ocular toxicity.
- Liposomal amphotericin B:
  - 3 mg/kg IV daily on days 1–5 and day 10 (total 18 mg/kg) is a commonly used regimen for CL when antimonials/miltefosine are unsuitable.
  - Monitor renal function and electrolytes; infusion reactions and hypokalemia can occur.
- Azoles (backup when preferred agents unavailable; variable efficacy):
  - Fluconazole 200 mg daily for 6 weeks showed benefit for L. major in some studies; monitor LFTs and drug interactions. Avoid in pregnancy.

Supportive care and follow-up
- Clean, cover, and protect from trauma; manage pain; treat bacterial superinfection if present.
- Sun protection over healing lesions to reduce hyperpigmentation.
- Expect slow healing even with treatment; reassess at 4–6 weeks. Scars are common.
- Old World species rarely cause mucosal disease; if any nasal/oral symptoms develop, seek urgent specialist review.

Special situations
- Pregnancy: avoid miltefosine; discuss risks/benefits of antimonials with a specialist. Liposomal amphotericin B is generally preferred if systemic therapy is needed.
- Children and immunocompromised patients: specialist management is recommended.

Get expert help
- Seek care with an infectious diseases or dermatology/tropical medicine specialist experienced in leishmaniasis. In the U.S., clinicians can consult the CDC Parasitic Diseases Branch for species testing and treatment guidance; in North Africa, referral centers commonly use intralesional or systemic antimonials and can advise on availability of miltefosine or thermotherapy.

If you can share more details (country, number/size of lesions, duration, any prior biopsy/PCR results, pregnancy status, immune conditions), I can help tailor the most appropriate regimen and next steps.

Rotina diária essencial
- Manhã
  - Escove por 2–3 minutos com pasta de dente. Use uma escova macia e pouca pressão.
  - Incline as cerdas a 45° para a margem da gengiva e faça movimentos curtos e suaves.
  - Limpe a língua com um raspador ou a própria escova.
  - Após escovar, evite enxaguar com muita água.

  - Depois, escove novamente como acima.

  - Use um enxaguante bucal adequado após as refeições, seguindo orientação profissional.

Ferramentas que ajudam
- Escova elétrica ajuda a reduzir mais placa e sangramento do que a manual. Troque cabeçote/escova a cada 3 meses.
- Entre os dentes:
  - Use escovas interdentais ou fio dental, conforme o espaço.
  - Irrigador oral pode ser um complemento útil.

- Pasta dental:
  - Escolha uma pasta dental adequada para suas necessidades, evitando opções muito abrasivas.

- Açúcar: limite a frequência de consumo. Evite “beliscar” o dia todo.

- Não escove com muita força; isso pode desgastar o esmalte e afetar a gengiva.

Check-ups e prevenção profissional
- Consulte um dentista regularmente para avaliação, limpeza que escova/fio não removem e orientações personalizadas.
- Selantes em sulcos de molares podem ajudar na prevenção de cáries.

- Noite: fio/escova interdental + escovar.

Stroke rehabilitation focuses on helping people relearn skills and regain independence after a stroke. It typically involves a multidisciplinary approach, with physical, occupational, and speech therapy playing key roles.

Some key points about stroke rehab:

- **Physical therapy**: Helps improve strength, balance, and coordination.
- **Occupational therapy**: Focuses on daily activities like dressing, bathing, and eating.
- **Speech therapy**: Aids recovery of speech and language skills if affected.
- **Emotional support**: Depression or anxiety can occur after a stroke, so counseling or support groups might be important.

Early and consistent rehabilitation can significantly improve outcomes, though progress can vary depending on the severity of the stroke and the person’s overall health.

Great—here’s a safe, structured home therapy plan after stroke. Adjust based on your abilities and what your rehab team has cleared you to do. 

**Daily Schedule (about 90–150 minutes total, broken into short blocks)**

- **Morning (20–30 min):** Breathing, gentle range-of-motion, sit-to-stand practice, short walk.
- **Midday (30–60 min):** Arm/hand therapy and a functional task (e.g., dressing, meal prep).
- **Afternoon (20–40 min):** Balance + gait work, then a 10–20 min endurance walk or bike.
- **Evening (10–20 min):** Long, slow stretches; speech/cognitive practice; relaxation.

**Upper Body (Affected Side)**

- **Range of Motion and Activation (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):**
  - Shoulder blade setting: gently pinch shoulder blades back and down.
  - Table slides: forearm on towel, slide arm forward and sideways.
  - Supported shoulder external rotation with elbow at side and a small towel roll.
  - Elbow bends/straightening; forearm pronation–supination.
  
- **Strength and Control (2–3 days/week):**
  - Theraband rows and pull-aparts; biceps curls; wrist extension.
  
- **Hand and Fine Motor (10–20 min daily):**
  - Putty squeezes, rolling, and pinches; clothespin transfers; coin pickup.
  
- **Functional Use:**
  - Reach to touch colored targets on a wall; fold towels; stack cups.
  
- **Optional:**
  - Mirror therapy (10–15 min): Mirror at midline, move non-affected hand while imagining affected hand moving the same.

**Shoulder Protection**

- Support arm on pillows when sitting/lying.
- Weight-bearing through the arm on a table with elbow straight.
- Gentle long-duration stretches for chest, biceps, and shoulder.

**Lower Body: Strength, Balance, and Gait**

- **Strength (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):**
  - Sit-to-stand from a chair; mini-squats; heel raises.
  
- **Ankle and Foot:**
  - Ankle pumps and alphabet; prolonged calf stretch.

- **Balance:**
  - Weight shifts at the counter; tandem stance with head turns.
  
- **Gait:**
  - Walk daily, starting with short bouts and building gradually.

**Spasticity and Tone Management**

- Slow, sustained stretches for affected muscles.
- Weight-bearing positions (arm on table).

**Edema and Skin Care**

- Elevate hand when resting; fist pumps and finger opens regularly.
- Gentle massage.

**Speech, Language, and Cognition**

- **Aphasia:** Naming items, describing pictures, reading short sentences aloud.
- **Dysarthria/Voice:** Speak loudly, over-articulate; practice phrases with strong breath support.
- **Cognitive:** Attention drills, memory tasks with reminders.

**Activities of Daily Living**

- One-handed techniques: hemidressing, adaptive utensils.
- Kitchen: Stabilize with non-slip mats.

**Endurance and Heart Health**

- Aim for continuous or interval cardio like walking or biking.

**Vision and Neglect (if present)**

- Visual scanning exercises.
- Place important items on the affected side.

**Progression and Goals**

- Set specific goals.
- Increase reps or time gradually as tolerated.

**Helpful Equipment**

- Therabands, therapy putty, reacher, sock aid.

**Caregiver Tips**

- Use techniques that protect the shoulder.

**Please Share:**

- Which side is affected and current mobility.
- Any concerns for further adjustments.

Safety first

- Stop and seek urgent care for new stroke signs (face droop, arm weakness, speech trouble), severe headache, chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or a painful swollen calf.
- Avoid pulling on the affected arm; don’t use overhead pulleys early on. Keep the shoulder supported.

- Afternoon (20–40 min): balance + gait work, then a 10–20 min endurance walk or bike.
- Evening (10–20 min): long, slow stretches; speech/cognitive practice; relaxation.
- Aim for most days of the week; stay at a “moderate” effort you can speak in short sentences.

- Range of motion and activation (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):
  - Shoulder blade setting: gently pinch shoulder blades back and down.
  - Table slides: forearm on towel, slide arm forward and sideways without hiking shoulder.
  - Supported shoulder external rotation with elbow at side and a small towel roll.
  - Elbow bends/straightening; forearm pronation–supination with a light hammer.

  - Finger extension with elastic band; repeated open–close for edema pumping.
- Functional use:
  - Reach to touch colored targets on a wall; fold towels; stack cups; open containers.
- Optional if safe: constraint-induced practice (30–120 min/day): restrain the stronger hand and do repetitive tasks with the affected hand—only if you can actively extend the wrist/fingers and have therapist clearance.
- Sensory and motor retraining:
  - Mirror therapy (10–15 min): mirror at midline, move non-affected hand while imagining affected hand moving the same.
  - Texture discrimination and object ID with eyes closed, then open.

- Support arm on pillows when sitting/lying; keep shoulder slightly forward and externally rotated.
- Weight-bearing through the arm on a table with elbow straight (30–60 seconds, 3–5 times).
- Gentle long-duration stretches (30–60 seconds) for chest, biceps, and shoulder.
- Use a sling only for walking if recommended; avoid hanging the arm unsupported.

Lower body: strength, balance, and gait
- Strength (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):
  - Sit-to-stand from a chair; mini-squats holding a counter; heel raises.
  - Bridges; side-lying clamshells; standing hip abduction/extension.
  - Step-ups to a low step; heel slides and straight-leg raises if needed.
- Ankle and foot:
  - Ankle pumps and alphabet; dorsiflexion with band; prolonged calf stretch.
  - If foot drop, practice heel strike and toe clearance; use AFO if prescribed.
- Balance (2–10 x 30–60 seconds):
  - Weight shifts forward/back and side-to-side at the counter.
  - Tandem stance (one foot in front of the other), then semi-tandem; head turns while standing.
  - Reaching tasks while standing; step and turn practice.
- Gait:
  - Walk daily, starting with short bouts (3–5 min) and building to 20–30 min.
  - Use a metronome app for consistent cadence if helpful. Focus on symmetrical steps and arm swing.

Spasticity and tone management
- Slow, sustained stretches for affected muscles (30–60 seconds, 3–5 reps): wrist/finger flexors, calf, hamstrings, hip adductors.
- Weight-bearing positions (arm on table, mini-squat holds).
- Gentle rhythmic rocking and deep breathing to reduce tone.
- Night hand/wrist splint or ankle neutral positioning device if provided.

Edema and skin care
- Elevate hand above heart when resting; fist pumps and finger opens 10–20 times hourly when awake.
- Gentle distal-to-proximal massage toward the elbow; consider a compression glove if advised.
- Check skin daily for redness, pressure spots, or breakdown—especially heels, hips, and affected hand.

Speech, language, and cognition (if affected)
- Aphasia (20–30 min/day): naming items in categories, describe pictures, read short sentences aloud; use apps like Constant Therapy or Tactus Therapy.
- Dysarthria/voice: speak loudly and slowly; over-articulate; practice counting or phrases with strong breath support.
- Cognitive: attention drills (find letters/numbers on a page), memory (use a notebook, phone reminders), problem-solving with simple tasks or apps.
- If swallowing is affected: eat sitting fully upright; small bites/sips; remain upright 30 minutes after; follow texture recommendations; meticulous oral care after meals.

Activities of daily living (practice daily)
- One-handed techniques: hemidressing (affected arm first on, last off), button hooks, elastic laces.
- Kitchen: stabilize with non-slip mats; slide items instead of lifting; use adaptive knives and rocker knives.
- Bathroom safety: grab bars, shower chair, hand-held shower, raised toilet seat. Never lock the bathroom door when alone.

Endurance and heart health
- 3–5 days/week of continuous or interval cardio at moderate effort: walking, recumbent bike, or arm ergometer.
- Warm up and cool down 5 minutes each. Hydrate. If you track BP and HR, follow your team’s parameters.

Vision and neglect (if present)
- Line bisection and visual scanning from the neglected side toward center using a bright left-edge anchor.
- Place important items on the affected side to encourage scanning and use.

Progression and goals
- Set 2–3 specific goals (e.g., “Walk 10 minutes without rest,” “Button a shirt in under 5 minutes”).
- Increase reps or time by 5–10% per week as tolerated; progress from supported to less supported tasks.
- Keep a simple log: what you did, time, difficulty, pain/fatigue, and any wins.

Helpful low-cost equipment
- Therabands, therapy putty, clothespins, cones/targets, pegboard, reacher, sock aid, long-handled sponge, balance pad, mirror, timer/metronome app.

Caregiver tips
- Use a gait belt for transfers; count down before moving.
- Protect the affected shoulder; never pull on the arm.
- Encourage independence but step in for safety.

Please share:
- Which side is affected and current mobility (walker/cane/no device)
- Any spasticity, pain, shoulder subluxation, or foot drop
- Speech or swallowing issues
- Equipment you have at home and time available
- Your top 2–3 goals

- Education and treat-to-target plan with your rheumatologist.
- Exercise: regular aerobic + strength training; hand therapy/OT for joint protection.

- Short courses of intra-articular steroid injections can help focal flares.

- Rapid symptom relief (short term only): 
  - NSAIDs as needed.
  - Glucocorticoids at the lowest dose for the shortest time; avoid chronic steroids.
- Conventional synthetic DMARDs (first-line):
  - Methotrexate is the anchor drug; consider subcutaneous route, split dosing, and folic acid to improve tolerance.
  - Alternatives/partners: leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine (triple therapy is effective and cost-conscious).
- Biologic DMARDs (add/switch if MTX inadequate):
  - TNF inhibitors: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab. Multiple adalimumab biosimilars now available with similar efficacy and often lower cost; interchangeability designations are expanding in the US.
  - IL-6 pathway inhibitors: tocilizumab, sarilumab. Useful as monotherapy if MTX-intolerant; can improve anemia and high CRP.
  - Abatacept (T-cell costimulation blocker): favorable in certain comorbidities (e.g., lung disease).
  - Rituximab (B-cell depleter): effective especially in seropositive RA and in certain cancer histories.
- Targeted synthetic DMARDs (oral JAK inhibitors):
  - Tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib provide rapid control. Due to class safety warnings (cardiovascular events, blood clots, malignancy), many guidelines suggest using them after TNF inhibitor failure or with careful risk stratification (extra caution if age >65, smokers, or high CV risk).

- Start methotrexate-based therapy; reassess in ~8–12 weeks.
- If not at target, add/switch to a biologic or JAK inhibitor based on comorbidities, preferences (injection vs oral), cost, and risks.
- Once stable remission for 6–12 months, consider cautious tapering (steroids first, then DMARDs), avoiding abrupt stops.

- Pregnancy/fertility: Avoid methotrexate and leflunomide; hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are generally safe; certolizumab is preferred among biologics. Plan therapy preconception.

- Heart failure: avoid TNF inhibitors in moderate–severe cases.
- Infections/hepatitis/TB risk: screen before biologics/JAKs; time vaccinations (especially before rituximab).

- Routine labs for methotrexate/leflunomide (CBC, LFTs), lipids for IL-6 blockers and JAK inhibitors, and infection surveillance.
- Minimize steroid exposure; bone protection if steroids needed (calcium/vitamin D, consider bisphosphonates).

What’s new or emerging
- Wider availability and interchangeability of adalimumab biosimilars is improving access.
- Growing use of ultrasound-guided treat-to-target tight control protocols.
- Risk-stratified use of JAK inhibitors based on updated safety data.

Evidence at a glance
- RCTs
  - ProPrems (Australia/NZ): Multistrain combo Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis Bb-02 + B. animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 + Streptococcus thermophilus TH-4 reduced NEC; no significant increase in sepsis.
  - PiPS (UK): Single-strain Bifidobacterium breve BBG-001 did not reduce NEC, sepsis, or death; raised issues about strain selection and product viability/colonization.
  - Numerous smaller RCTs with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103) and with Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium combinations suggest NEC reduction; effects appear larger with multistrain products and in predominantly human-milk–fed cohorts.

  - Consistently show reduced NEC (relative risk roughly 0.5–0.7) and a modest reduction in mortality; effect on late-onset sepsis is neutral or small. Guidelines and positions

Out-of-network coverage refers to health care services you get from providers who do not have a contract with your insurance company. When you receive care from an out-of-network specialist, several steps usually happen:

1. **Provider Charges**: The specialist sets a rate, which can be higher than the in-network negotiated rate.
2. **Insurance Submission**: You or the provider may need to submit a claim to your insurance for reimbursement.
3. **Plan Reimbursement**: Your insurance plan might reimburse only a portion of the billed amount (or even nothing, depending on your plan’s rules).
4. **Patient Responsibility**: You pay any remaining balance, which may be higher than what you’d pay for in-network care.

It’s common for out-of-network specialists to charge you directly, leaving you to handle insurance claims on your own. Always review your insurance plan’s summary so you know how they handle out-of-network claims and what portion of the costs you’ll owe.

If you use an out-of-network specialist, you’ll usually pay more than in-network. Your cost can include an out-of-network deductible, higher coinsurance, and “balance billing” (the difference between what the provider charges and what your plan allows). Yes, you can often negotiate a cash/self-pay rate, especially if you can pay upfront.

What you might have to pay:

- Plan type matters:
  - HMO/EPO: Often no out-of-network coverage except for true emergencies. You could owe the full bill unless you get an authorized exception/referral.
  - PPO/POS: Usually covered, but at worse terms.

- Typical out-of-network cost components:
  - Separate, higher out-of-network deductible (must be met before the plan pays).
  - Higher coinsurance on the plan’s “allowed amount.”
  - Balance billing: You may owe the difference between the provider’s charge and your plan’s allowed amount.
  - Possible preauthorization penalties if you didn’t get required approval.

- Out-of-pocket maximums:
  - Out-of-network often has a separate, higher out-of-pocket max, and many plans don’t count balance bills toward it.

- Legal protections:
  - Emergencies and certain services at in-network facilities are protected by the No Surprises Act: you pay only in-network cost-sharing and cannot be balance-billed.

Can you negotiate a cash rate?

- Often yes. Many specialists offer a self-pay or “prompt pay” discount, especially if you pay at the visit.

- How to ask:

Scalp tenderness without rash or itching is common and often not serious. The most frequent causes are:
- Traction or pressure on hair follicles from tight ponytails/buns, clips, extensions, helmets, or headsets
- “Trichodynia” (scalp sensitivity) linked to stress, tension headaches, or neck/shoulder strain
- Recent increased shedding or new hair growth after illness, weight loss, COVID, postpartum, or medication changes
- Mild sun/wind burn or irritation from new hair products

A few quick questions to narrow it down:
- Do you wear tight hairstyles, extensions, or headgear for long periods?
- Have you noticed more hair shedding lately?
- Any headaches, jaw clenching, or neck/shoulder tightness?
- Did you start new shampoos, dyes, or scalp treatments?
- Is the tenderness in one area or all over? Any broken hairs or thinning along the hairline?

What you can try now (usually helps within 1–2 weeks):
- Avoid traction: skip tight styles, heavy clips, and sleeping in a ponytail; wear hair loose.
- Be gentle: use a wide-tooth comb, hold hair near the roots while brushing to reduce pull; avoid vigorous scrubbing.
- Simplify products: use a gentle, fragrance-free shampoo; avoid harsh dyes, bleaching, or heat styling for now.
- Soothe: warm shower or warm compress, then gentle fingertip massage (not nails) for 5–10 minutes daily.
- Address tension: posture breaks, gentle neck/shoulder stretches, and manage stress/sleep.
- Sun protection: hat or scalp-safe sunscreen along your part if you’ve had sun exposure.

When to seek care:
- No improvement after 1–2 weeks of avoiding traction and being gentle
- Patchy hair loss, broken hairs along the hairline, or a receding hairline (possible traction alopecia)
- Severe or one-sided burning pain followed by a rash/blisters (possible shingles) or any swelling, warmth, pus, fever
- Frequent severe headaches, neurologic symptoms, or very tender lumps that don’t go away
- Ongoing heavy shedding (to check for thyroid/iron or other causes)

If you’d like, you can share a photo of the most tender area and describe your typical hairstyle routine and any recent changes—those details can help pinpoint the cause and next steps.

- Indications: Symptomatic, tense, or progressive subcutaneous emphysema despite conservative care.

- Noncontrast CT to exclude hemorrhage; perform CTA head/neck up-front in most suspected AIS to detect LVO. Don’t delay CTA for creatinine in emergent stroke unless clear contraindications.
- Perfusion imaging: Use if considering EVT beyond 6 hours or in unclear eligibility; MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch supports thrombolysis in wake-up strokes.

- IV thrombolysis (IVT):

- Mechanical thrombectomy (EVT):
  - Standard: Proven anterior-circulation LVO within 0–6 hours; up to 24 hours with perfusion or clinical–core mismatch (DAWN/DEFUSE 3).
  - Large-core updates (2023–2024): SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT support EVT benefit even with large cores (low ASPECTS 3–5 or core volumes ≥50–70 mL in selected patients).

- Time targets:
  - Door-to-CT start ≤15 min; door-to-needle ≤30 min (at least ≤45 min); door-to-groin ≤60 min for EVT candidates.
- Practical: Mix-and-bolus at CT; one-stop imaging-angiography suites if available; pharmacy prepares TNK/altplase at scanner.

4) Blood pressure, glucose, and supportive care
- Before IVT: <185/110 mmHg; after IVT: ≤180/105 mmHg for 24 hours.
- After EVT:
  - If successful reperfusion (e.g., mTICI 2b–3): target SBP ~120–140 mmHg; avoid <120 due to harm seen in trials.
  - If poor/no reperfusion: permissive higher range 140–180 mmHg; individualize to cerebral perfusion needs.
- Glucose: Treat hyperglycemia; goal 140–180 mg/dL. Avoid hypoglycemia.
- Temperature: Treat fever promptly; normothermia improves outcomes.
- Oxygen: Supplemental O2 only if SpO2 <94%.
- DVT prophylaxis: Intermittent pneumatic compression on arrival; start pharmacologic prophylaxis after 24 hours if post-IVT CT shows no hemorrhage.

- Neuro checks and BP per protocol (e.g., q15 min ×2 h, q30 min ×6 h, q1 h ×16 h).

Sorry you’re dealing with this—abdominal pain with intermittent diarrhea is common, but the one-time blood in the stool is a sign to pay attention to.

Possible causes:
- Infection (viral or bacterial “stomach bug,” foodborne illness, or parasites), often causes cramping, diarrhea, sometimes fever; can irritate the rectum and cause light bleeding.
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D): crampy pain and diarrhea that comes and goes, often triggered by stress or certain foods; typically does NOT cause bleeding.
- Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/ulcerative colitis): abdominal pain, diarrhea, urgency, mucus, and blood.
- Hemorrhoids or an anal fissure: bright red blood on toilet paper or on the surface of the stool, often with pain on wiping or after straining/diarrhea.
- Other causes could be medication effects, lactose intolerance/celiac disease, or, less commonly, diverticular disease or polyps.

When to seek urgent care now:
- Heavy bleeding, black/tarry stools, or repeated bleeding.
- Severe or worsening abdominal pain, fever, fainting/lightheadedness, fast heartbeat, shortness of breath, or signs of dehydration (very thirsty, minimal urine).
- Vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down, or vomiting blood.

What to do next (non-urgent but important):

Here’s a quick, WHO-aligned approach for a healthy adult with 1 day of diarrhea and mild dehydration.

How much to give
- If no/suspected minimal dehydration (Plan A): After each loose stool, drink about 200–250 mL of ORS. Aim for at least 2–3 liters of total fluids in 24 hours, more if thirsty.
- If mild/some dehydration: Give 75 mL/kg of ORS over the first 4 hours, then reassess. For adults this is typically 3–5 liters over 4 hours (example: 70 kg ≈ 5 L). After correction, continue 200–250 mL ORS after each loose stool.
- If vomiting: give small, frequent sips (30–60 mL every 5 minutes). If vomiting occurs, pause 5–10 minutes and resume.

What ORS is (reduced-osmolarity WHO/UNICEF formula)
- Per 1 liter of clean water:
  - Sodium 75 mmol/L (as sodium chloride 2.6 g)
  - Chloride 65 mmol/L
  - Potassium 20 mmol/L (as potassium chloride 1.5 g)
  - Citrate 10 mmol/L (as trisodium citrate dihydrate 2.9 g)
  - Glucose (anhydrous) 75 mmol/L (13.5 g)

How to mix and administer
- Use one standard ORS sachet per exactly 1 liter of clean/safe water. Stir until fully dissolved. Do not concentrate or dilute.

- If no sachet is available: mix 6 level teaspoons of sugar + 1/2 level teaspoon of salt in 1 liter of clean water (it should taste “no more salty than tears”). Use only level measures.

Diet and what to avoid
- Continue normal diet as tolerated; include salty broths and potassium-rich foods (e.g., bananas). Avoid alcohol, undiluted fruit juice, sodas/energy drinks, and very sweet beverages.

- Reassess after 4 hours. If signs of dehydration are not improving, if oral intake is not tolerated, or if there are any concerns like persistent vomiting or blood in stool, seek medical care promptly. Consider earlier escalation for older adults or those with additional health concerns.

- DTaP protège contre: diphtérie, tétanos et coqueluche (pertussis). La coqueluche est particulièrement dangereuse chez les nourrissons, d’où le début précoce des vaccins.

- Pourquoi ces âges:
  - 2 mois: première dose pour amorcer la protection.
  - 4 mois: renforcement de la réponse.
  - 6 mois: complète la série primaire pour une bonne immunité la première année.
  - 15–18 mois: rappel, car l’immunité diminue; il prolonge la protection chez le tout-petit.

- Et après: une 5e dose est généralement prévue à 4–6 ans, puis un rappel Tdap vers 11–12 ans, et ensuite un rappel tétanos/diphtérie (Td ou Tdap) tous les 10 ans. Pendant chaque grossesse, un Tdap est recommandé pour protéger le nouveau-né.

- Peut-on l’administrer avec d’autres vaccins: oui, souvent en vaccins combinés (par ex. avec polio, Hib, hépatite B). C’est courant et sûr.

- Si une dose est en retard: on reprend là où on s’est arrêté, sans recommencer toute la série. Des intervalles minimaux existent (en général 4 semaines entre les 1res doses et ~6 mois avant le rappel), mais ton pédiatre te guidera.

- Effets secondaires fréquents: douleur/rougeur au point d’injection, irritabilité, somnolence.

  - Réaction allergique grave à une dose précédente ou à un composant: contre-indication.
  - Encéphalopathie inexpliquée dans la semaine suivant une dose contenant la coqueluche: on évite la composante “aP”.
  - Maladie légère (rhume) = OK; maladie modérée/sévère = on peut différer.

- Prématurés: on vaccine selon l’âge chronologique (pas besoin d’attendre), car ils sont plus à risque de coqueluche.

- Petits conseils pratiques:
  - Surveillance après l’injection; compresse froide si douleur.

What’s often confusing is that many soft tissue tumors are not sarcomas:
- Benign soft tissue tumors: lipoma, hemangioma, schwannoma, etc.

- Malignant: soft tissue sarcomas (can be low-, intermediate-, or high-grade; even low-grade sarcomas are still malignant, just slower-growing with lower metastatic risk).

- Deep to the muscle fascia
- Growing over time
- Painful or recurrent after prior removal

- Chart choice:

  - Correct for prematurity (generally to 24 months for weight/length; consider to 24–36 months for head circumference in some practices).

  - Weight-for-age or weight-for-length/height z-score decline ≥1.0 within 2–3 months (infants) or within 6 months (toddlers/children).
  - Crossing down two major percentile lines.
  - WLZ/BMI-for-age < −2 SD, or height-for-age z-score < −2 SD (stunting).
  - Subnormal height velocity for age.
- Core message: verify measurements, plot correctly, assess velocity and pattern (weight vs length/height vs head circumference), then intervene early; reserve labs for red flags or poor response.

Practical approach you can start now
1) Re-check the basics (especially if you’re seeing this in multiple patients)
- Equipment and technique: calibrated scale, infant length board or wall-mounted stadiometer, no shoes/heavy clothes, repeat measures and average.
- Make sure everyone is plotting on WHO 0–24 months and CDC 2–20 years consistently, with corrected age for preterm infants.

2) Stratify the pattern
- Weight drops first, length/height preserved: most often inadequate intake or increased needs/losses.
- Length/height velocity slows disproportionately: consider endocrine or chronic disease.
- Head circumference deceleration: consider neurologic or genetic conditions.

- Diet/feeding routines, formula preparation, breast milk supply, feeding skills, mealtime dynamics, juice/milk displacement, food insecurity.

- Concerning social situation or possible neglect.

- Dietitian for most cases needing catch-up growth.

Short answer: there isn’t one universal number, but major health bodies agree kids should keep added/free sugars very low.

What most guidelines say
- Under 2 years: avoid added sugars entirely (AAP, Dietary Guidelines for Americans).
- Ages 2–18:
  - Simple cap: keep added sugars at or below 25 grams per day (about 6 teaspoons) and avoid sugary drinks (American Heart Association).
  - Percent of calories: keep added/free sugars under 10% of daily calories; even better under 5% (WHO; also used in UK guidance).
    - Example: if a child eats 1,500 kcal/day, 10% = ~150 kcal from sugar ≈ 37 g; 5% ≈ 19 g.

Regional examples
- UK (Public Health England, based on 5% energy):
  - Ages 4–6: ≤19 g/day
  - Ages 7–10: ≤24 g/day
  - Ages 11+: ≤30 g/day

Key definitions
- Added sugars: sugars added during processing or at the table (sucrose, HFCS, honey, syrups).
- Free sugars (WHO/UK): added sugars plus sugars naturally present in juice, honey, and syrups.
- Naturally occurring sugars in whole fruit and plain milk are not limited the same way; whole fruit is encouraged.

Practical tips
- Drinks: choose water and plain milk. Limit 100% fruit juice; it counts as free sugar.
- Label check: use the “Added Sugars” line. 4 grams = 1 teaspoon.
- Quick context: a 12-oz soda has ~35–40 g added sugar (already over the AHA daily cap).

If you share your child’s age and typical calorie needs or eating pattern, I can help set a concrete daily target and suggest swaps that fit your family.

Here’s a practical guide to flossing—what to use, how to do it right, and how to handle special situations.

**Why floss**
- Removes plaque and food between teeth and under the gumline where brushes can’t reach.
- Helps prevent cavities between teeth, gum disease, and bad breath.

**How to floss (standard string floss)**
1. Take 18 inches (45 cm) of floss. Wrap most around one middle finger and the rest around the other, leaving 1–2 inches to work with.
2. Hold the floss taut with your thumbs and index fingers.
3. Gently guide it between teeth with a slight sawing motion—don’t snap it down onto the gums.
4. Curve the floss into a C-shape around one tooth. Slide it up and down 5–10 strokes, going just under the gumline.
5. Keeping tension, hug the neighboring tooth and repeat.
6. Use a fresh section of floss for each space. Don’t forget the back of your last molars.
7. Rinse after. Brushing after flossing helps fluoride reach between teeth.

**How often and when**
- Once daily is the minimum; nighttime is ideal.
- Order: floss then brush for better fluoride delivery, but consistency matters more than order.

**Common mistakes to avoid**
- Snapping floss into the gums.
- Not going under the gumline on each tooth.
- Reusing the same dirty section of floss.
- Stopping because gums bleed: mild bleeding is common at first and usually improves in 3–7 days with daily flossing.

**What to use: picking the right tool**
- String floss: waxed, unwaxed, tape, PTFE. Use what you’ll use daily.
- Floss picks/holders: easier for many people. Use a gentle in-and-out with a C-curve; wipe the pick or switch sides as you go.
- Interdental brushes: tiny bottle-brush tools. Often better than floss if you have gaps, gum recession, or periodontal issues. Ask a hygienist for the right size.
- Water flossers: helpful for braces, implants, dexterity issues, or sensitive gums. Aim at the gumline; go tooth to tooth for 1–2 minutes. They complement, not replace, brushing.

**Special situations**
- Braces/retainers: use floss threaders or orthodontic/super floss to get under wires. Interdental brushes around brackets and a water flosser can make it much easier.
- Bridges: thread floss under the bridge (use super floss) and clean the underside of the false tooth.
- Implants: use implant-safe floss/super floss and nylon-coated interdental brushes.
- Gum disease/recession: interdental brushes sized to your spaces are often most effective. Your hygienist can size them.
- Kids: start flossing when teeth touch (often age 2–6). Caregivers should help until good hand skills develop (around 8–10). Kids’ floss picks can help.
- Sensitive or bleeding gums: start gently; improve technique.

**Troubleshooting**
- Floss shreds or catches: could indicate a rough filling, tartar, or a cavity—see your dentist.
- Pain or persistent bleeding, swelling, bad taste/odor, loose teeth, or pus: seek dental care promptly.

**Quick routine to try tonight (about 2–3 minutes)**
- Floss every space with the C-shape technique.
- Brush for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste.
- Optionally rinse.

Short answer: yes—postpartum follow-up at home or in primary care is normal in Spain. Spain typically discharges earlier and shifts much of routine postnatal care out of the hospital.

How it usually works in Spain:
- Hospital stay: 
  - Uncomplicated vaginal birth: about 24–48 hours.
  - Cesarean: about 48–72 hours.
- After discharge:
  - A midwife (matrona) and/or community nurse from your local health center (centro de salud) follows up. In many areas they call you and see you within 24–72 hours; some regions offer a home visit, others schedule you at the clinic.
  - Newborn check: a pediatrician visit is usually arranged in the first few days, plus the newborn screening “prueba del talón” (day 3–5), often at the health center or hospital.
  - Breastfeeding support and maternal recovery (stitches, bleeding, pelvic floor, mood) are handled by the matrona and primary care team. 

How this differs from Germany:
- Germany’s Hebamme system standardizes home visits after discharge.
- Spain has similar support via the public primary care matrona/nurse, but home visits vary by autonomous community; some places rely more on clinic visits. Private “matrona a domicilio” and lactation consultants are also common if you want extra home support.

Tips if you’re delivering in Spain:
- Before discharge, ask about “alta precoz” protocols and whether your area offers a home visit.
- Book the first pediatric and matrona appointments through your centro de salud as soon as you have the baby’s health card details.

If you tell me your region (e.g., Madrid, Catalonia, Andalusia), I can outline what’s typical there and how to set it up.

- Go to urgent care today if you have any of: obvious deformity, severe swelling, inability to move fingers, numbness/tingling/weakness, the hand looks pale/cold/blue, or marked tenderness in the snuffbox.

- Position: Lay the child supine with legs elevated unless vomiting or in respiratory distress (then semi-recumbent), and remove the trigger if possible.

- ≥30 kg: 0.3 mg autoinjector.

- Hypotension or shock: Isotonic crystalloid bolus 20 mL/kg; repeat as needed.

Your description (multiple, nonhealing ulcers on the arms in a desert setting in North Africa) suggests Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis, often due to *Leishmania major* in that region. Management involves confirming the diagnosis.

What to do now:
- Get diagnostic confirmation: ideally PCR with species ID from a lesion sample. Acceptable tests include a slit-skin smear or scraping, punch biopsy, or aspirate.

- Basic wound care: gentle saline cleansing, nonadherent dressings, avoid topical steroids, treat secondary bacterial infection only if present.

When to treat versus observe:
- Many *L. major* lesions heal spontaneously over 2–6 months but leave scars.

First-line options for Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis:

Local therapy (preferred for small, uncomplicated lesions):

Tested positive for a BRCA gene

A positive BRCA test often means a significantly increased lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. It indicates that your DNA contains changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes, which normally help repair damaged DNA.

Physician recommended prophylactic mastectomy or close surveillance

Prophylactic (preventive) mastectomy is a surgical option that can reduce the risk of breast cancer by removing most of the breast tissue. This step is sometimes taken when the estimated risk is very high. On the other hand, close surveillance typically involves frequent mammograms, MRIs, and clinical exams to detect cancer early if it develops.

Both approaches can be valid, but the best choice varies based on factors like your personal risk profile and preferences regarding surgery and potential complications. A discussion with a specialist or genetic counselor is often recommended to weigh all the considerations.

Close surveillance can be effective if you remain diligent with mammograms, MRIs, and regular exams, but it doesn’t reduce risk—only catches potential cancers early. Balancing the impact on your quality of life, psychological well-being, and medical considerations is key. Compare dryness from reading physical books and dryness from working on a computer for me

Dry eye sensations can arise in both situations, but using digital screens often leads to more frequent dryness because of reduced blinking and prolonged focus. Here is a short comparison:

1. **Blink Rate**
   - **Reading Physical Books**: When reading, you generally maintain a steadier blink rate, though it can still decrease if you’re deeply focused.
   - **Using a Computer**: Screen-based activities often reduce your blink rate further, partially due to the visual demand and glare.

2. **Screen Glare & Brightness**
   - **Physical Books**: Glare can be an issue under direct light, but it’s often easier to control by adjusting the book’s position or lighting.
   - **Computer Screens**: The constant light source and glare from monitors can contribute to eye fatigue, which may exacerbate dryness.

3. **Viewing Distance**
   - **Physical Books**: Typically read at a comfortable arm’s length, which can reduce strain.
   - **Computer Screens**: Viewing distance may be longer, and the eyes might be working harder to focus on pixels.

4. **Body Position**
   - **Physical Books**: You might shift your posture more often while reading a book, possibly putting less continuous strain on certain eye muscles.
   - **Computer Screens**: People often sit in a fixed posture for extended periods, which can lead to less blinking and an increase in dryness.

5. **Environmental Factors**
   - **Physical Books**: Reading is more flexible with lighting; you can easily step away or take breaks.
   - **Computer Screens**: Work environments may have air conditioning or heating that affects humidity around your workspace.

Overall, both activities can cause dryness if done for extended periods without breaks. However, prolonged computer use often intensifies dryness due to reduced blinking and constant exposure to a lit screen.
give me best tips for dryness from extended screen time. don't give me cliche advice. I'm 35 with no medical issues, want recognized standard approaches

Here are evidence-based, non-cliché strategies to reduce screen-related dryness. Pick a few that fit your routine and try them consistently for a couple of weeks.

1) Lower your gaze and shrink the eyelid opening
- Position the top of your monitor at or slightly below eye level and tilt the screen back slightly. Looking slightly downward covers more of the eye with the upper lid, reducing tear evaporation.
- Increase text size and viewing distance. Larger, easier-to-read text reduces staring and incomplete blinks.

2) Blink quality training (not just “blink more”)
- Every 20–30 minutes, do 10 “complete blinks”: close fully, gently squeeze for 1 second, open slowly. Many screen users have partial blinks; this retrains full lid closure and spreads oil across the tear film.
- Use a subtle nudge: a desktop timer, watch vibration, or app that flashes a tiny dot every 20–30 minutes to cue the blink set.

3) Control evaporation and airflow
- Keep humidity 40–50% with a desk humidifier. Move AC/heat vents so air doesn’t flow across your face.
- If your eyes feel better outdoors or with higher humidity, consider moisture-chamber eyewear like clear wraparound frames. These can markedly cut evaporation in dry offices.

4) Lighting that reduces visual demand
- Add diffuse lighting behind/around the monitor to reduce glare and the bright-screen/dark-room contrast that causes staring. Aim for 300–500 lux ambient light.
- Use matte screen protectors and position the screen to avoid window reflections.

5) Optimize the screen itself
- Use a larger, higher-PPI external monitor over a small laptop screen. Set a higher refresh rate if available.
- Choose a clear, high-contrast theme and enlarge fonts. Use a well-lit light mode if dark mode causes squinting.

6) Smart lubrication
- Use preservative-free artificial tears during heavy screen use. Use them consistently rather than waiting for discomfort.
- If mornings are rough, consider a preservative-free gel at bedtime for added moisture overnight.

7) Meibomian gland support
- Apply a warm compress for 5–10 minutes once or twice daily with a microwaveable eye mask, then gently massage along the lid margins. This improves the oil layer and slows evaporation.

8) Practical work-habit changes
- Pair short microbreaks with posture and blink resets: stand up, look mid-distance, do 10 complete blinks, relax shoulders/neck, then resume.
- Voice input for long emails or notes can reduce continuous visual demand.

9) Avoid hidden dryness amplifiers
- Point fans away from your face.

By implementing these strategies, which target screen-related causes, you should notice an improvement in discomfort and dryness.

Stroke rehab

Stroke rehabilitation focuses on helping people relearn skills and regain independence after a stroke. It typically involves a multidisciplinary approach, with physical, occupational, and speech therapy playing key roles.

Some key points about stroke rehab:

- **Physical therapy**: Helps improve strength, balance, and coordination.
- **Occupational therapy**: Focuses on daily activities like dressing, bathing, and eating.
- **Speech therapy**: Aids recovery of speech and language skills if affected.
- **Emotional support**: Depression or anxiety can occur after a stroke, so counseling or support groups might be important.

Early and consistent rehabilitation can significantly improve outcomes, though progress can vary depending on the severity of the stroke and the person’s overall health.
Home therapy plan

Great—here’s a safe, structured home therapy plan after stroke. Adjust based on your abilities and what your rehab team has cleared you to do. 

**Daily Schedule (about 90–150 minutes total, broken into short blocks)**

- **Morning (20–30 min):** Breathing, gentle range-of-motion, sit-to-stand practice, short walk.
- **Midday (30–60 min):** Arm/hand therapy and a functional task (e.g., dressing, meal prep).
- **Afternoon (20–40 min):** Balance + gait work, then a 10–20 min endurance walk or bike.
- **Evening (10–20 min):** Long, slow stretches; speech/cognitive practice; relaxation.

**Upper Body (Affected Side)**

- **Range of Motion and Activation (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):**
  - Shoulder blade setting: gently pinch shoulder blades back and down.
  - Table slides: forearm on towel, slide arm forward and sideways.
  - Supported shoulder external rotation with elbow at side and a small towel roll.
  - Elbow bends/straightening; forearm pronation–supination.
  
- **Strength and Control (2–3 days/week):**
  - Theraband rows and pull-aparts; biceps curls; wrist extension.
  
- **Hand and Fine Motor (10–20 min daily):**
  - Putty squeezes, rolling, and pinches; clothespin transfers; coin pickup.
  
- **Functional Use:**
  - Reach to touch colored targets on a wall; fold towels; stack cups.
  
- **Optional:**
  - Mirror therapy (10–15 min): Mirror at midline, move non-affected hand while imagining affected hand moving the same.

**Shoulder Protection**

- Support arm on pillows when sitting/lying.
- Weight-bearing through the arm on a table with elbow straight.
- Gentle long-duration stretches for chest, biceps, and shoulder.

**Lower Body: Strength, Balance, and Gait**

- **Strength (8–12 reps x 2–3 sets):**
  - Sit-to-stand from a chair; mini-squats; heel raises.
  
- **Ankle and Foot:**
  - Ankle pumps and alphabet; prolonged calf stretch.

- **Balance:**
  - Weight shifts at the counter; tandem stance with head turns.
  
- **Gait:**
  - Walk daily, starting with short bouts and building gradually.

**Spasticity and Tone Management**

- Slow, sustained stretches for affected muscles.
- Weight-bearing positions (arm on table).

**Edema and Skin Care**

- Elevate hand when resting; fist pumps and finger opens regularly.
- Gentle massage.

**Speech, Language, and Cognition**

- **Aphasia:** Naming items, describing pictures, reading short sentences aloud.
- **Dysarthria/Voice:** Speak loudly, over-articulate; practice phrases with strong breath support.
- **Cognitive:** Attention drills, memory tasks with reminders.

**Activities of Daily Living**

- One-handed techniques: hemidressing, adaptive utensils.
- Kitchen: Stabilize with non-slip mats.

**Endurance and Heart Health**

- Aim for continuous or interval cardio like walking or biking.

**Vision and Neglect (if present)**

- Visual scanning exercises.
- Place important items on the affected side.

**Progression and Goals**

- Set specific goals.
- Increase reps or time gradually as tolerated.

**Helpful Equipment**

- Therabands, therapy putty, reacher, sock aid.

**Caregiver Tips**

- Use techniques that protect the shoulder.

**Please Share:**

- Which side is affected and current mobility.
- Any concerns for further adjustments.

- Lasts longer than 2 weeks, can start anytime in the first year

Here’s a concise, up-to-date overview of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treatment as of 2024–2025. The goal is remission or low disease activity using a treat-to-target approach and regular reassessment.

- Education and treat-to-target plan with your rheumatologist.

- Rituximab (B-cell depleter).

How treatment is sequenced:
- Start methotrexate-based therapy; reassess.
- Add/switch to a biologic or JAK inhibitor based on individual considerations.
- Once stable remission, consider cautious tapering.

Special clinical situations:
- Pregnancy/fertility: Plan therapy preconception.
- Interstitial lung disease: Consult your specialist.
- Heart failure: Discuss options with your rheumatologist.
- Infections/hepatitis/TB risk: Follow appropriate screening and vaccination guidelines.

Monitoring and safety:
- Routine labs for methotrexate/leflunomide and infection surveillance.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this—dizziness plus shortness of breath can have many causes. Most are not dangerous, but some need prompt evaluation. Let’s triage and figure out next steps.

Red flags – seek urgent care (call emergency services or go to ER) if any of these occur:
- Chest pain/pressure, tightness, or pain spreading to arm/jaw/back
- Fainting or near-fainting, new confusion, trouble speaking, one-sided weakness, severe headache
- Severe shortness of breath at rest, blue lips, or inability to speak full sentences
- Fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn’t settle
- Coughing up blood or one-sided calf swelling/pain with sudden breathlessness
- Shortness of breath that wakes you from sleep or is much worse when lying flat
- Possible carbon monoxide exposure (headache, dizziness in multiple people in same space)

Common possible causes when symptoms come and go:
- Dehydration, low blood pressure, or orthostatic intolerance (symptoms when standing up)
- Inner ear/vestibular issues (BPPV), vestibular migraine
- Anxiety/panic with hyperventilation
- Viral illness (including COVID), asthma flare
- Anemia (low red blood cells/iron), especially with heavy periods or recent blood loss
- Heart rhythm issues, less commonly heart disease

Bottom line
- Evidence shows that prophylactic probiotics can reduce necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and all-cause mortality in very preterm/VLBW infants. The effects vary by strain selection, product quality, feeding practices, and baseline NEC rates.

Evidence at a glance
- Meta-analyses indicate reduced NEC and a modest reduction in mortality. Effects on late-onset sepsis are neutral. Benefits are most consistent with Bifidobacterium combinations.

Guidelines and positions
- ESPGHAN supports considering L. rhamnosus GG or the ProPrems three-strain combination, emphasizing strict product quality assurance and monitoring.
- WHO advises consideration in settings with high baseline NEC and quality-assured strains.

Strain selection: what has the best support
- Multistrain combinations (B. infantis Bb-02 + B. lactis BB-12 + S. thermophilus TH-4) have strong evidence.
- L. rhamnosus GG is favorable in several analyses.

Practical implementation if you proceed
- Ensure high human-milk feeding rates and NEC surveillance capability.
- Select strains with RCT support, source from quality-assured manufacturers, and prepare in a pharmacy clean area.
- Consider treatment for VLBW once minimal enteral feeds are established.

- Track NEC, mortality, and feeding tolerance. Reassess the program regularly.

Controversies and knowledge gaps
- Optimal strain(s), dose, and duration are not fully defined. Multistrain products with Bifidobacterium show consistent benefits. Generalizability to settings with low baseline NEC or high donor-milk use may affect outcomes.

Key references (selected)
- ProPrems RCT and PiPS RCT demonstrate different efficiency and outcomes.
- ESPGHAN position paper and Cochrane reviews summarize evidence on strain effects.
- WHO and Canadian Paediatric Society provide guidelines on probiotic use in preterm infants.

- Disfunción temporomandibular, problemas dentales.
- Cervicalgia, contracturas, neuralgia occipital.

Condiciones médicas generales

- Anemia, trastornos tiroideos.
- Hipertensión severa (crisis).
- Trastornos autoinmunes.
- Trastornos del sueño.

What is out-of-network coverage and how is it different from in-network coverage

Out-of-network coverage refers to health care services you get from providers who do not have a contract with your insurance company. Because they don’t have a set agreement with your insurer, these providers often charge more than in-network providers, and you may be responsible for a higher portion of the costs.

In contrast, in-network coverage applies to providers who have negotiated rates with your insurance plan. This typically results in lower out-of-pocket costs for you, such as reduced copays or coinsurance. When using in-network providers, you often benefit from the insurance company’s discounted rates, which is why it’s usually more cost-effective to stay in-network.
How does the billing process typically work if I see an out-of-network specialist

When you receive care from an out-of-network specialist, several steps usually happen:

1. **Provider Charges**: The specialist sets a rate, which can be higher than the in-network negotiated rate.
2. **Insurance Submission**: You or the provider may need to submit a claim to your insurance for reimbursement.
3. **Plan Reimbursement**: Your insurance plan might reimburse only a portion of the billed amount (or even nothing, depending on your plan’s rules).
4. **Patient Responsibility**: You pay any remaining balance, which may be higher than what you’d pay for in-network care.

It’s common for out-of-network specialists to charge you directly, leaving you to handle insurance claims on your own. Always review your insurance plan’s summary so you know how they handle out-of-network claims and what portion of the costs you’ll owe.
Is there a separate deductible for out-of-network services or does it share the same one as in-network

Many plans have two different deductibles: one for in-network services and another, often higher, for out-of-network care. If you see an out-of-network specialist, you usually must meet that separate (and typically higher) out-of-network deductible before your insurance begins to cover any portion. Some plans, however, might track in-network and out-of-network spending under a single combined deductible, but that’s less common.

It’s important to check your policy or contact your insurer directly to see which system your plan uses. This can help you estimate how much you’ll pay if you go out-of-network.
What portion might I have to pay, and can I negotiate a cash rate with the specialist

If you use an out-of-network specialist, you’ll usually pay more than in-network. Your cost can include an out-of-network deductible, higher coinsurance, and “balance billing” (the difference between what the provider charges and what your plan allows). Yes, you can often negotiate a cash/self-pay rate, especially if you can pay upfront.

What you might have to pay:

- Plan type matters:
  - HMO/EPO: Often no out-of-network coverage except for true emergencies. You could owe the full bill unless you get an authorized exception/referral.
  - PPO/POS: Usually covered, but at worse terms.

- Typical out-of-network cost components:
  - Separate, higher out-of-network deductible (must be met before the plan pays).
  - Higher coinsurance on the plan’s “allowed amount.”
  - Balance billing: You may owe the difference between the provider’s charge and your plan’s allowed amount.
  - Possible preauthorization penalties if you didn’t get required approval.

- Out-of-pocket maximums:
  - Out-of-network often has a separate, higher out-of-pocket max, and many plans don’t count balance bills toward it.

- Legal protections:
  - Emergencies and certain services at in-network facilities are protected by the No Surprises Act: you pay only in-network cost-sharing and cannot be balance-billed.

Can you negotiate a cash rate?

- Often yes. Many specialists offer a self-pay or “prompt pay” discount, especially if you pay at the visit.

- How to ask:
  - Request their self-pay cash price and any prompt-pay discount before you book.
  - Ask for CPT/procedure codes to compare prices.
  - Propose a bundled, all-in price and ask if they’ll accept it as “payment in full.”
  - Get the offer in writing, including what’s included.

Important notes:

- If you use a cash price, you generally can’t also submit to insurance.
- Hospitals and some large groups have financial assistance policies—ask if you qualify.

How to estimate your cost before you go:

- Call your insurer:
  - Is this service covered out-of-network? Any preauthorization needed?
  - What are my out-of-network deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket max?
  - What is the allowed amount for these CPT codes with this provider/ZIP?

- Call the specialist:
  - Total cash price and what it includes; payment options/discounts; whether they balance bill; whether they will submit claims if you choose to use insurance.
If I have really frequent gout flares how can I use hydrogen water for that

Short answer: There isn’t good evidence that hydrogen (H2) water reduces uric acid or prevents gout flares. If you want to try it, use it only as an add-on to proven gout care, not a replacement.

If you still want to use hydrogen water:
- Dose and strength: Most studies that looked at general wellness used ~1–2 liters per day of hydrogen-rich water at about 1–1.6 ppm dissolved H2.
- Timing: Sip throughout the day. Drink it soon after preparation or opening (within 15–30 minutes) because hydrogen dissipates quickly.
- Preparation: Use a reputable generator or tablets with third-party testing for H2 concentration. Store in a sealed, non-permeable container to limit gas loss.
- Expectations: It may help hydration, but it has not been proven to lower serum urate or reduce flares. Track what matters: serum urate level and flare frequency.

What will help most with frequent flares:
- Achieve target uric acid levels with recommended urate-lowering therapies guided by healthcare professionals.
- Maintain hydration: 2–3 liters of fluids daily is beneficial. Plain water is as effective as hydrogen water for hydration.
- Diet and triggers: Limit beer/spirits and high-fructose corn syrup; minimize organ meats and large portions of red meat. Favor low-fat dairy, vegetables, and coffee (if tolerated).
- Lifestyle: Gradual weight loss, addressing sleep patterns, and managing overall health can help.

If you share your current goals and lifestyle, suggestions can be made to pair evidence-based care with anything you want to try, including hydrogen water, and a simple way to track progress.
hi i think there's something weird with my scalp . it's been feeling kinda sore especially when i brush or comb my hair . i want to know if it's normal or if i might have some scalp issue .

i’m here to help, and i appreciate you sharing what’s going on . can you tell me more about this soreness ? do you notice any redness or itching on your scalp ? or is it mainly just tender whenever you move your hair around ?

there isn’t any rash or itching . it’s more like a dull tenderness that happens mostly when i pull my hair back or brush it . i’m worried i might be damaging my hair or that there's some hidden condition i don’t know about . i could really use some advice .

Scalp tenderness without rash or itching is common and often not serious. The most frequent causes are:
- Traction or pressure on hair follicles from tight ponytails/buns, clips, extensions, helmets, or headsets
- “Trichodynia” (scalp sensitivity) linked to stress, tension headaches, or neck/shoulder strain
- Recent increased shedding or new hair growth after illness, weight loss, COVID, postpartum, or medication changes
- Mild sun/wind burn or irritation from new hair products

A few quick questions to narrow it down:
- Do you wear tight hairstyles, extensions, or headgear for long periods?
- Have you noticed more hair shedding lately?
- Any headaches, jaw clenching, or neck/shoulder tightness?
- Did you start new shampoos, dyes, or scalp treatments?
- Is the tenderness in one area or all over? Any broken hairs or thinning along the hairline?

What you can try now (usually helps within 1–2 weeks):
- Avoid traction: skip tight styles, heavy clips, and sleeping in a ponytail; wear hair loose.
- Be gentle: use a wide-tooth comb, hold hair near the roots while brushing to reduce pull; avoid vigorous scrubbing.
- Simplify products: use a gentle, fragrance-free shampoo; avoid harsh dyes, bleaching, or heat styling for now.
- Soothe: warm shower or warm compress, then gentle fingertip massage (not nails) for 5–10 minutes daily.
- Address tension: posture breaks, gentle neck/shoulder stretches, and manage stress/sleep.
- Sun protection: hat or scalp-safe sunscreen along your part if you’ve had sun exposure.

When to seek care:
- No improvement after 1–2 weeks of avoiding traction and being gentle
- Patchy hair loss, broken hairs along the hairline, or a receding hairline (possible traction alopecia)
- Severe or one-sided burning pain followed by a rash/blisters (possible shingles) or any swelling, warmth, pus, fever
- Frequent severe headaches, neurologic symptoms, or very tender lumps that don’t go away
- Ongoing heavy shedding (to check for thyroid/iron or other causes)

If you’d like, you can share a photo of the most tender area and describe your typical hairstyle routine and any recent changes—those details can help pinpoint the cause and next steps.

What are the possible reasons behind feeling a faint numbness in the left arm?

Possible reasons for a faint numbness in the left arm include:

1. **Nerve Compression or Irritation**: Issues like carpal tunnel syndrome or pressure on a nerve in the neck or shoulder region can manifest as tingling or numbness.

2. **Circulatory Factors**: Reduced blood flow from vascular problems or compression of blood vessels can cause numbness.

3. **Posture or Overuse**: Sitting with poor posture, repetitive movements, or sleeping on the arm can cause this sensation.

4. **Potential Underlying Conditions**: In rare cases, heart-related issues might present with arm numbness, though it typically involves other symptoms.

Individual factors such as how long the numbness lasts, whether it’s worsening or accompanied by pain, and any personal medical history can also be important considerations.
Could it be serious enough that I should see a doctor immediately, or can I just wait to see if it goes away on its own?

Short answer: it depends on the context and any other symptoms.

Seek emergency care now (call your local emergency number) if the numbness is accompanied by any of the following:
- Chest pressure/pain, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain in the jaw/neck/back (possible heart issue).
- Sudden trouble speaking, facial droop, severe headache, new confusion, or weakness in one side of the body (possible stroke/TIA).
- Rapidly worsening weakness in the arm/hand, inability to grip or lift, or numbness after a neck/back injury.
- The arm/hand becomes very pale/blue, cold, or very painful (possible circulation issue).
- New loss of bladder/bowel control or severe neck/back pain with electric-shock sensations.

Contact your doctor soon (same day or within 24–48 hours) if:
- The numbness persists longer than a day or two, keeps coming back, or is getting worse.
- You notice weakness, clumsiness, dropping objects, or neck/shoulder pain that radiates down the arm.
- There’s swelling, redness, visible veins in the arm, fever, or a new rash (e.g., shingles).
- You have diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, or other relevant medical conditions.
- The symptom occurs with exertion or emotional stress, especially if you have heart risk factors.

It’s reasonable to watch and see if it improves on its own if:
- The numbness is faint, intermittent, clearly linked to position or pressure (e.g., sleeping on the arm, leaning on the elbow), and you feel otherwise well.
- It eases within minutes to hours after changing posture and doesn’t come with weakness or other symptoms.

Self-care while observing:
- Avoid positions that compress the neck, shoulder, elbow, or wrist; take frequent breaks from repetitive tasks.
- Keep the wrist neutral (a night wrist splint can help if symptoms suggest carpal tunnel).
- Gentle neck and shoulder stretches; heat or ice as preferred.

If you’d like, tell me:
- When it started, how long it lasts, what brings it on or relieves it.
- Any chest discomfort, shortness of breath, facial droop, speech trouble, headache, neck pain, weakness, or hand clumsiness.
- Your age and any heart risk factors (smoking, high BP, diabetes, high cholesterol, family history).
Patient post-radiation therapy now exhibiting crepitus on palpatiion of chest wall.

Crepitus on the chest wall post-radiation therapy suggests subcutaneous emphysema, where air becomes trapped under the skin. It's essential to assess the extent and underlying cause to determine the appropriate management.
Chest X-ray confirms widespread subcutaneous emphysema, no evideence of pneumothorax.

In the absence of pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema may resolve spontaneously. However, if extensive or causing discomfort, intervention may be necessary. Monitoring the patient's respiratory status is important.
Patient's oxygen saturation stable, but sweling causes discomfort; considering air release.

If the patient is stable but experiences discomfort due to subcutaneous emphysema, air release can be considered. This involves inserting a device to allow trapped air to escape, but the procedure must be conducted aseptically, especially in immunocompromised patients.
Seeking guidance on minimally invasive techniques for air eavcuation in such cases.

Needle puncture or small incisions with insertion of subcutaneous drains can help evacuate trapped air. In immunocompromised patients, the procedure should be performed under sterile conditions, with prophylactic antibiotics if indicated.
Optimal needle gauge and insertion points for subcutaneous emphysema drainage in immunocomprimised patient.

Short answer
- Needle/catheter size: 14–16 G angiocatheters for simple decompression; 8–14 Fr fenestrated subcutaneous drains (e.g., JP/pigtail) if ongoing evacuation is needed.
- Insertion sites: Bilateral infraclavicular anterior chest wall, about 2–3 cm below the clavicle along the midclavicular to anterior axillary line, placed strictly in the subcutaneous plane at sites of maximal crepitus. Keep the catheter parallel to the skin and superficial to avoid pleural violation and neurovascular structures. Use ultrasound to confirm depth and avoid vessels. Favor closed systems.

Practical considerations for an immunocompromised patient
- Indications: Symptomatic, tense, or progressive subcutaneous emphysema despite conservative care.
- Preferred approach: Closed percutaneous drainage.

Technique tips (for trained clinicians)
- Preparation: Full sterile technique, chlorhexidine prep, drape; ultrasound to map subcutaneous thickness and avoid vessels (esp. internal mammary near sternum, subclavian deep to clavicle, external jugular/branches in neck).
- Device choice:
  - 14–16 G angiocatheters (2–4 catheters) for initial decompression in thin/moderate habitus.
  - 8–14 Fr fenestrated subcutaneous drains tunneled 5–10 cm in the subcutis for ongoing evacuation or obese patients.
- Insertion locations:
  - Chest wall: Start bilaterally in the infraclavicular region, 2–3 cm inferior to the clavicle, midclavicular to anterior axillary line, targeting the most fluctuant/crepitant areas. Direct the catheter tangentially and keep within the subcutaneous layer (advance only 1–2 cm for angiocaths).
  - Additional sites: Upper anterior axillary line or upper lateral chest if air tracks laterally.
  - Neck involvement (if clinically needed): Consider very superficial placement near the suprasternal notch or along the anterior border of SCM above the clavicle only with ultrasound guidance and caution due to vascular structures.
- Drainage setup:
  - Connect to a closed system: low continuous suction (e.g., JP bulb or -5 to -10 cm H2O) or a one-way valve.
  - Secure with suture/adhesive device; apply occlusive dressing.
- Alternatives/escalation:
  - If massive or refractory: short “blow-hole” incisions (1–2 cm) in the infraclavicular area with negative-pressure wound therapy over the incision to create a sealed system.

Aftercare and precautions
- Monitor for clinical improvement and reduction in crepitus; repeat chest imaging if symptoms change.
- Remove drains once air leak subsides (no drainage/crepitus progression for 24 hours).
- Frequent dressing changes and skin checks (radiated skin is fragile).
- Reassess for underlying causes if persistent (e.g., occult tracheobronchial or pleural injury) even if initial CXR shows no pneumothorax.

im a sports medicine doc want the new stepwise protocol for concussion return to play referencing the updated consensus statement

Here’s the updated stepwise Return-to-Sport (RTS) strategy aligned with the 6th International Consensus on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022; published 2023 in BJSM). It emphasizes early, symptom-limited activity rather than strict rest, structured aerobic progression, and a formal clearance checkpoint before contact.

**General principles**
- Initial 24–48 hours: relative rest, not strict rest. Allow activities of daily living and light, symptom-limited physical/cognitive activity; limit prolonged screen time and high cognitive load.
- Progression: minimum 24 hours per step. Most athletes require at least 1 week before contact practice, longer in youth.
- Symptom response rule: mild, brief symptom increases can be acceptable during early stages; if symptoms are more than mild or persist >1 hour, stop, return to prior step after 24 hours symptom stability, and progress more gradually.
- Return-to-learn/work should be prioritized; non-contact exercise can progress in parallel. Full contact and game play require symptom resolution at rest and with exertion.

**Stepwise Return-to-Sport progression**
- **Step 1: Symptom-limited activity (24–48 h)**
  - Light ADLs, brief walks, gentle mobility. Aim: gradual re-introduction of physical and cognitive activity without worsening symptoms.

- **Step 2A: Light aerobic exercise**
  - Intensity: up to about 55% of age-predicted HRmax; RPE ~2–3/10.
  - Examples: walking, easy stationary cycling, light swimming. No resistance training.

- **Step 2B: Moderate aerobic exercise**
  - Intensity: up to about 70% of HRmax; RPE ~4–5/10.
  - Examples: brisk walk, moderate spin, short intervals below symptom threshold. Still no impact.

- **Step 3: Sport-specific exercise (no head-impact risk)**
  - Add movement and individual sport skills: running/skating drills, footwork, ball work without risk of contact.
  - Light resistance training can begin/progress as tolerated.

- **Step 4: Non-contact training drills**
  - More complex, high-intensity drills; multidirectional movements; controlled reaction/decision-making.
  - Progress resistance training and conditioning.

- **Medical clearance checkpoint (before Step 5)**
  - Criteria: resolution of symptoms at rest and with exertion; neurological, vestibulo-ocular, and balance examinations at or back to baseline.

- **Step 5: Full-contact practice**
  - Normal training sessions after medical clearance. Monitor for symptom recurrence.

- **Step 6: Return to competition**
  - Full game play.

**Special considerations**
- Adolescents/children: progress more conservatively (often ≥48 hours per step). Expect longer timelines (often 2–4+ weeks). Prioritize return to school within 1–2 days; adjust academic load as needed.
- Persisting symptoms (>2–4 weeks adults; >4 weeks youth) or clear symptom profiles: initiate targeted, multidisciplinary rehab (e.g., cervicovestibular therapy, vision therapy, supervised sub-symptom aerobic exercise).

**Monitoring tools**
- SCAT6/Child SCAT6 for acute and serial assessments.
- SCOAT6/Child SCOAT6 for office-based, subacute evaluation.

If you want, I can provide a one-page handout version (clinic-ready) with progress criteria and a symptom monitoring checklist aligned with SCAT6 terminology.
Help me understand this “I just slipped in my yard and landed on my side my hip is sore but i can still walk i’m worried i might have a fracture.”

Short answer: Being able to walk doesn’t rule out a hip or pelvic fracture. Many falls like this are bruises or strains, but small or non-displaced fractures can still let you walk and need imaging to confirm.

What to watch for right now
- Concerning signs (go to urgent care/ER today): 
  - Inability to bear weight or pain that sharply worsens with each step
  - Leg looks shorter or turned outward, or obvious deformity
  - Severe pain in the groin (not just the outer hip) after the fall
  - Significant swelling/bruising spreading quickly
  - Numbness, weakness, or new trouble moving the leg
  - You’re 65+ or have osteoporosis
  - You also hit your head, lost consciousness, or have headache, confusion, or vomiting

If none of the above apply
- Arrange an in-person evaluation within 24–48 hours to be safe. You may need an X-ray; if it’s normal but pain is still significant, a CT or MRI may be needed to rule out a hairline fracture.
- Rest and protect the hip: avoid running, jumping, lifting, or long walks.
- Ice the sore area 15–20 minutes at a time, every 2–3 hours for the first 48 hours.
- Use a cane or crutch on the opposite side to reduce load on the hip.

Clues about what it might be
- More likely a bruise/soft-tissue injury: tenderness mainly over the outer bony part of the hip (side), pain improves with rest, you can bear weight with only mild/moderate pain.
- More concerning for a fracture: pain deep in the groin or front of hip, pain with each step or when lifting the leg, pain worsening overnight or at rest.

A few quick questions to help gauge risk
- Where exactly is the pain (outer side vs groin/front)?
- How old are you, and do you have osteoporosis?
- Can you bear weight on that leg for 4 steps?
- Any head strike, dizziness, or loss of consciousness?
- Is the pain getting better, worse, or about the same since the fall?
